title: Weak \(\varepsilon\)-net size exponent
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge2\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:f_d(\varepsilon)=O_d(\varepsilon^{-a})\text{ as }\varepsilon\downarrow0\}.\] The function \(f_d(\varepsilon)\), defined below, is the worst-case minimum cardinality of a weak \(\varepsilon\)-net hitting all convex sets that contain at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of a finite point set in \(\mathbb R^d\). Net points may lie outside the input set. The requested answer concerns the exponent, with no requirement to determine logarithmic factors.
why: Weak nets quantify how many representatives can preserve every large convex part of an arbitrary finite configuration. Sharp bounds would settle a basic gap in discrete geometry and clarify the geometric cost underlying transversal, selection and approximation results.
status_note: The extremal asymptotic question is open in the checked sources, including the higher-dimensional revision of December 2023. The bounded later-work review on 13 September 2026 did not find matching bounds for the stated family. Publication and revision dates are distinguished from the date of this status check.

sentences: A weak epsilon-net hits every convex set containing a sufficiently large fraction of the input points.
Its chosen points may lie anywhere in Euclidean space.
The question asks how the worst-case net size grows as a power of inverse accuracy.
The exponent is requested to absolute error 0.01 in every fixed dimension.
The target imposes no algorithmic construction requirement and ignores logarithmic factors.

definitions: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be any nonempty finite set of distinct points, and let \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) be real. A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net is a finite set \(N\subset\mathbb R^d\) such that \(N\cap C\ne\varnothing\) for every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(|P\cap C|\geq\varepsilon|P|\). A set is convex if it contains the segment joining any two of its points. All convex ranges, including unbounded and lower-dimensional ones, are allowed; no restriction to halfspaces, simplices or a given finite family is made. Equivalently it is enough to hit \(\operatorname{conv}(Q)\) for every \(Q\subseteq P\) with \(|Q|\geq\lceil\varepsilon|P|\rceil\), so using only closed convex ranges gives the same condition. Net points can lie anywhere in \(\mathbb R^d\) and need not belong to \(P\). Put \(w(P,\varepsilon)=\min\{|N|:N\text{ is a weak }\varepsilon\text{-net for }P\}\) and \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\subset\mathbb R^d,\,0<|P|<\infty}w(P,\varepsilon)\). The minimum exists since \(N=P\) is feasible. The supremum ranges over every size and configuration with the same fixed dimension and accuracy; a bound depending on \(|P|\) is not a bound on \(f_d\). The weak-net theorem ensures \(f_d(\varepsilon)<\infty\). There is no general-position, rational-coordinate, uniform-measure-on-space, algorithmic or randomized guarantee in the target: the only measure is the uniform counting measure on the given finite set. The problem measures extremal cardinality, not construction time. For each fixed integer \(d\ge2\), define \[x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \exists\varepsilon_0\in(0,1/2]\ \forall\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_0],\ f_d(\varepsilon)\le C\varepsilon^{-a}\}.\] Constants may depend on \(d\) and \(a\), but not on the accuracy or point set. The classical polynomial upper bound and inverse-accuracy lower bound give \(1\le x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)\le d\), so every requested value is a finite real number. The infimum need not be attained; a polylogarithmic factor in \(1/\varepsilon\) does not change the exponent. Different fixed dimensions may use different constants, with no uniform bound on their growth requested.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously specified real answer \(a(d)\) for every integer \(d\ge2\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of absolute error at most \(1/100\) in the defined exponent. A certified enclosing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. Both sides of the interval must be justified. An exact value also qualifies. The infimum need not be attained, and no ordinary logarithmic growth limit is assumed. Matching logarithmic factors, leading constants and an algorithm attaining the endpoint exponent are not required. A one-sided improvement alone qualifies only if the resulting certified interval is sufficiently narrow.

context_blocks.text: The source asks for the true asymptotic behavior of weak-net size in every fixed dimension. The owner’s numerical-target rule selects its polynomial exponent in inverse accuracy, rather than matching the entire function within constant factors.

A strong net is required to choose its points from the input. Allowing auxiliary points is essential for arbitrary convex ranges: arguments for bounded-complexity range families do not automatically supply weak nets for all convex sets.

Bukh, Matoušek and Nivasch prove the general lower bound \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\Omega_d(\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d-1}(1/\varepsilon))\). In particular, already in the plane a universal bound proportional to \(1/\varepsilon\) is impossible.

Rubin improves the planar upper bound to \(O_\gamma(\varepsilon^{-3/2-\gamma})\) for every fixed \(\gamma>0\). The constant can depend on \(\gamma\); this theorem is not the assertion of an \(O(\varepsilon^{-3/2})\) bound with a uniform constant.

Rubin’s higher-dimensional work, including its December 2023 revision, improves the previously known upper bounds in all fixed dimensions at least three. Those bounds still do not match the lower bound above. Their dependence on dimension does not turn the problem into a joint large-dimension asymptotic question.

The same net must hit all heavy convex ranges simultaneously. Choosing a different auxiliary point after seeing each range would be a different and trivial requirement. This simultaneous coverage is what makes the extremal bound relevant to geometric transversals and sampling.
